capitals.name: Thimphu (Tashichho Dzong; Cheri and Simtokha in the Thimphu valley)

ledger.x: 1616: the Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal arrives from Tibet and founds the Drukpa state in western Bhutan.
1634: the unification of Bhutan is complete.
1650: the Druk Desi period begins: after the Zhabdrung's death (1651, kept secret for 54 years) secular rule passes to the Druk Desi under the dual system with the Je Khenpo.
1700: Bhutan invades Sikkim again.
1706: the fighting for the Kalimpong hills ends with Bhutanese control.
1706: Bhutan takes Kalimpong from Sikkim.
1765: Bhutan treats Cooch Behar as its dependency.
1765: Bhutan seizes direct control of Cooch Behar's Jalpeswar, Mandas and Jalash.
1772: the East India Company comes to Cooch Behar's aid against Bhutan.
ledger.cpn: British Empire in India (East India Company rule)

ledger.x: 1773: Cooch Behar passes to the East India Company.
April 1774: Bhutan makes peace with the East India Company.
ledger.cpn: British Empire in India (East India Company rule)

ledger.x: April 1774: Bhutan gives up its Cooch Behar holdings.
1784: the British hand the Bengal Duars back to Bhutan.
ledger.cpn: British Empire in India (East India Company rule)

ledger.x: About 1790: the Druk Desi takes the Assam (Darrang) Duars from the declining Ahom kingdom.
1841: the East India Company annexes the Assam Duars.
ledger.cpn: British Empire in India (East India Company rule)

ledger.x: 1864: the Duar War begins between British India and Bhutan.
11 November 1865: the Treaty of Sinchula ends the Duar War.
11 November 1865: Bhutan cedes the Duars and the Kalimpong hills to British India.
11 November 1865: Bhutan cedes Dewangiri to British India.
17 December 1907: Ugyen Wangchuck becomes Bhutan's first hereditary king and the Druk Desi system ends.
August 1949: India returns Dewangiri to Bhutan with the Treaty of Friendship.

wars.name: Tibetan and Mongol invasions of Bhutan
wars.outcome: All repelled: no land changed hands.

wars.name: Bhutan-Koch Bihar war of 1711
wars.outcome: The Bhutan page says only '1711, Bhutan went to war with the Raja of Koch Bihar'; no result is given, and 'in the 18th century, Bhutan invaded and occupied Koch Bihar'.

wars.name: Tibetan and Mongol invasion of Bhutan (1714)
wars.outcome: 'In 1714 Tibetan forces, aided by Mongolia, invaded Bhutan but were unable to gain control' (History of Bhutan); the Bhutan page: 'Tibetans unsuccessfully attacked Bhutan'.

wars.name: Bhutanese invasions of Sikkim and the Kalimpong hills
wars.outcome: Kalimpong 'is said to have come under the control of Bhutan in the year 1706', after 'Bhutanese encroachments' lasting about two decades.

wars.name: Bhutanese-British war over Cooch Behar
wars.outcome: The British drove the Bhutanese garrison out of Cooch Behar; the peace of 25 April 1774 required Bhutan to return to its pre-1730 boundaries and pay a tribute of five horses.

wars.name: Bhutanese civil wars
wars.outcome: The Bhutan page: 'Civil war between Paro and Tongsa' in the 1870s-1885; 'Ugyen Wangchuck united the country during 1882-85'; History of Bhutan: 'several civil wars and rebellions in 1882-85'.

wars.name: Duar War
wars.outcome: British victory: the Treaty of Sinchula, 11 November 1865, cedes the Eighteen Duars, the Teesta hill territory and Dewangiri (83 km2); Bhutan loses a fifth of its territory and receives 50,000 rupees a year.

certainty.note: Highland frontiers with Tibet and Sikkim are approximate; the plains frontier in the Duars moved with the dependency of Cooch Behar (1765-1774) and the 1784 hand-back; no survey line is given by any page opened.

The southern frontier follows the Treaty of Sinchula (1865, 'points laid down by the British Commissioner') and the 1949 return of Dewangiri; the northern frontier with Tibet and China is approximate, and about 269 km2 remain disputed…
